profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a fintech market-surveillance startup after the first internal deployment of a pump-and-dump detector for Poloniex-listed tokens produced too many analyst alerts over the weekend. The context is that the team expected the thresholding-plus-EWMA model to suppress harmless micro-cap noise, but the review queue still filled with low-value incidents, especially on thinly traded tokens that had been inactive for days. The agenda is to diagnose why the detector is still generating noisy alerts, determine whether the issue is in the threshold logic, baseline calculations, or alert packaging, and agree on a practical fix that can be shipped before the next compliance review. The expected outcome is an action plan for a 'threshold recalibration' update and a shared belief that the alert problem is understood well enough to proceed without a larger redesign.

members.name: Leah Chen
members.expertise: Surveillance workflows, analyst operations, alert triage, compliance-facing product delivery
members.background: Leah previously worked in transaction monitoring at a digital-asset compliance vendor and now manages the internal alert-review product used by the startup's surveillance analysts.
members.private_state: She needs to reduce analyst complaint volume quickly before a quarterly compliance demo, and wants a narrow fix that preserves the current model narrative rather than reopening architecture decisions.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says an alert is 'actionable,' it means a human analyst can review it quickly and find enough contextual signal to decide whether to escalate.
A 'pump event' should correspond to a token-level incident bundle, not multiple separate line items created by clustered spikes in the same token over a short period.
The 'inactive token' problem mainly concerns tokens with no meaningful trading for several calendar days, because those are what analysts perceive as dead markets suddenly waking up.
If they 'recalibrate thresholds,' the work should stay within alerting behavior and tuning parameters, not change upstream data windows or event grouping logic.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Time-series anomaly detection, market microstructure, feature engineering, production model tuning
members.background: Arjun has a quantitative trading research background and built the EWMA- and volatility-based detector now running in the startup's surveillance pipeline.
members.private_state: He wants to defend the core model design, show that the detector is mathematically sound, and avoid adding ad hoc product-layer exceptions that could distort evaluation of the algorithm.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says an alert is 'actionable,' it means the scored event meets the statistical abnormality threshold strongly enough to deserve analyst attention, regardless of review convenience.
A 'pump event' is each threshold-crossing interval produced by the detector, even if several occur on the same token within a few hours.
An 'inactive token' is one with near-zero recent observations inside the rolling baseline window, not necessarily one that has been quiet across multiple calendar days.

If they 'recalibrate thresholds,' it is acceptable to change baseline construction details such as EWMA decay, warm-start behavior, and window eligibility because those are part of thresholding behavior.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an actionable alert
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the detector should produce only 'actionable alerts.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah means alerts that are packaged and sparse enough for analysts to review efficiently, with enough token-level context that most can be dispositioned in one pass.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun means alerts whose underlying score exceeds the intended anomaly threshold with statistical credibility, even if many are tedious or redundant for analysts to process.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In surveillance teams, 'actionable' is a standard positive term that sounds shared and practical; both members sincerely endorse it, and neither expects the other to attach a different success criterion because both criteria usually correlate in normal discussions.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to reducing duplicate 'pump events' on the same token.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah treats a pump event as one token-level incident episode, so three spikes in ZEPH/USDT over two hours should be grouped into one analyst-facing case.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun treats a pump event as each qualifying 15-minute interval that independently breaches price and volume thresholds, so those same three spikes are legitimately three events.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term 'event' is common in both product and modeling contexts and usually passes without definition; because both are discussing the same token and same time period, surface agreement feels complete even though the unit of counting differs.

misalignment_points.topic: Which inactive-token behavior is causing the noise
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss 'the weekend inactive-token alerts,' especially examples like dormant micro-cap tokens suddenly moving.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah is thinking of tokens that had been practically dead for several days and then generated a visible burst on Sunday, matching analyst complaints about 'zombie coins.'
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun is thinking of tokens whose 48-period rolling baseline had decayed toward zero overnight, even if the token traded modestly the previous day, because that is what produced threshold sensitivity in his logs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are referring to the same broad class of thin-liquidity weekend alerts and may even mention similar token names, so it is easy to assume they mean the same subset when in fact they are anchoring on different concrete instances from different diagnostics.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to do a 'threshold recalibration' before the next review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah assumes recalibration means adjusting exposed trigger cutoffs and perhaps deduplication settings while leaving baseline generation and detector mechanics intact.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun assumes recalibration includes changing the EWMA decay factor, warm-up handling for sparse series, and volatility floor logic because those define how thresholds behave on illiquid assets.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a modest technical tuning step rather than a design boundary; since both see themselves as preserving the same model family, neither notices that one includes upstream statistical machinery while the other assumes only downstream trigger parameters.

We need a narrow fix: tune alert behavior, reduce duplicate analyst-facing cases, and get the volume down so the alerts feel actionable in the review workflow.
